analysis.one_liner: Makes it harder to sue companies for securities fraud while adding new audit and fraud-detection rules.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 1994 with 21 Senate cosponsors from both parties, the bill never left the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how investors sue companies for securities fraud. It would tighten the rules for bringing those lawsuits — requiring more detailed claims, shortening the time limit, limiting each defendant's share of damages, and barring most fraud-in-securities cases under the anti-racketeering law. At the same time it would add investor protections: auditors would have to hunt for illegal acts at companies they audit and report them, a new self-disciplinary board would police accounting firms, and class-action lawyers would face new limits on referral fees and payouts.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies and their executives gain the most: they would face fewer and harder-to-win investor lawsuits, a safe harbor for optimistic forward-looking statements, and capped liability if other wrongdoers can't pay. Auditors gain liability protection for reporting fraud, though they also take on new duties and fees. Ordinary investors gain in narrower ways: auditors would have to detect and disclose illegal acts, settlements would have to be disclosed, and lawyers could no longer take referral fees for rounding up clients.

how_it_helps.text: Auditors would have to include procedures designed to detect illegal acts, identify material related-party transactions, and evaluate whether a company can keep operating, and report detected illegal acts up to the board and ultimately the SEC [S2][S3].
A new Public Auditing Self-Disciplinary Board would register accounting firms and investigate and discipline firms that violate securities laws or professional standards [S2][S3].

Brokers would be barred from taking referral fees for steering customers to securities-fraud lawyers, class attorneys' fees would be capped as a share of what the class actually recovers, and settlement terms would have to be disclosed to class members [S2][S3].
Named class plaintiffs could no longer take outsized recoveries, and a court-appointed guardian or class-member committee would oversee counsel and settlements [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Investors who bought stock based on false statements would bear the main cost: stricter pleading rules, a shorter two-year-from-discovery filing window, damages capped at the corrected-price difference, and proportionate liability — meaning if the main wrongdoer is insolvent, the other defendants generally pay only their own share, with extra payment required only in narrow cases. Companies and accounting firms would pay for new audit procedures, board registration fees, and exposure to discipline.

drawbacks.text: The bill sets a strict filing deadline — generally two years after the fraud was discovered or five years after it occurred — which would cut off claims by investors who learn of fraud late [S2][S3].

It requires plaintiffs to plead specific facts showing each defendant's state of mind and to spell out each allegedly misleading statement before discovery, a hurdle that is difficult to clear when evidence is in the company's hands [S3].

It replaces joint-and-several liability with proportionate liability for most defendants, so if the central wrongdoer cannot pay, investors may collect only a fraction of their losses; the safety valve applies only to individuals whose damages exceed 10% of a net worth under $200,000 [S3].
It excludes securities fraud from the RICO anti-racketeering law, eliminating treble-damages claims against fraudulent issuers [S2][S3].

The proposed auditing board would be financed by accounting firms themselves, with four of seven members elected by certified public accountants — industry self-policing rather than independent oversight [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs real investor protections — mandatory fraud-detection audits and public reporting of illegal acts — with significant curbs on investors' ability to sue and recover. The litigation curbs are the larger half of the bill: shorter deadlines, tougher pleading, capped damages, and proportionate liability all shift the balance toward companies and away from defrauded shareholders. An honest reading is that the audit provisions are the strongest part and the lawsuit restrictions the weakest, and they pull in opposite directions.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate referred it to the Banking Committee, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the bill on March 24, 1994, joined by Senators Domenici, Mikulski, Johnston, and Faircloth [S1][S3][S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day [S5].
The record shows no further action — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died without a vote, the pre-existing rules for securities fraud suits stayed in place, which favored defrauded investors and the plaintiffs' bar; companies gained nothing from the proposed lawsuit curbs but also avoided the new mandatory audit and self-disciplinary regime.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 21 cosponsors split 13 Republicans to 8 Democrats, so sponsorship crossed party lines; the record shows no organized opposition, only committee inaction.

industries.industry: Publicly traded companies and corporate executives
industries.note: Tighter pleading rules, a safe harbor for forward-looking statements, proportionate liability, shorter filing deadlines, and the RICO exclusion all reduce companies' exposure to investor fraud suits. Investors' recoveries are the mirror image of those savings.

Auditors would gain a liability shield for fraud-related reports and would run the new self-disciplinary board, but they would face mandatory fraud-detection procedures, registration fees, and SEC-backed discipline. This self-regulatory design locks auditors in as the gatekeepers of their own oversight.

The bill bars lawyer referral fees from brokers, caps fees as a share of class recovery, requires disclosure of settlements, and adds loser-pays penalties for unreasonable positions — shrinking the fees and practices of the plaintiff bar while aiming at practices criticized as abusive.
Brokers would be banned from soliciting or accepting referral fees for steering customers to securities-fraud lawyers, removing a kickback channel that directly cost class members.
